activity: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
knowledge_domain: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
story:
Lily sat at Grandma's big table. She wanted to write her name all by herself. Grandma put a pencil in her hand. But Lily held it way up high. The pencil slipped. Her lines came out wiggly and light. "That is not my name," said Lily.

Grandma showed her how to pinch the pencil down low, near the point. Lily tried it. She pressed down. The pencil did not slip. A dark line stuck to the paper and stayed there. "It stays!" said Lily. She made a big L. Then an i with a dot. Then l and y. There it was. L-I-L-Y.

Lily held up the paper. "Look, Grandma! My name!" Grandma clapped. "Can I write it again?" Lily asked, pulling a fresh sheet from the empty tray. Outside, a car went by on the street, but Lily did not look up. She was busy making letters.

activity: starting the first day of school
knowledge_domain: starting the first day of school
story:
Henri woke up early. The sun made a bright triangle on his wall. Today was his first day of school. He did not want to go. He hid his shoe under the bed.

"Where is your shoe?" Mama asked. Henri pointed at the cat. "The cat chased it," he said. Mama looked under the bed. She found the shoe. "Let's put it on," she said.

Henri stamped his feet. His shoes made a happy sound. Stomp, stomp, stomp. Then the cat ran to him. The cat liked the sound too. The cat chased Henri's feet all the way to the door. Henri laughed.

Mama held his hand. They walked to school. The cat sat on the step and waved its tail.

At school, Henri saw a big rug. It had red triangles on it. He sat down on a red triangle. A boy next to him smiled. "I like your shoes," the boy said.

Henri looked at his shoes. They still made a happy sound. He stomped one foot, soft and small. The boy stomped too.

"Henri, time for juice," the teacher said. Henri ran to the table. He was wide awake now. "Mama will come back," the teacher said. "After juice and songs."

Henri drank his juice. He sang the songs. Then the door opened. It was Mama. Henri ran fast. "I stomped and made a friend," he said.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
knowledge_domain: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Josephine went to the park with her grandma. She wanted to find a duck to feed. She held grandma's hand the whole way. Stay close, stay close, that was their game.

Near the pond, Josephine saw a grill. It was smoking. A kind man was cooking corn on it. "Is it fire?" Josephine asked. "Yes, a little fire," said grandma. "Fire is hot. We look with our eyes only." Josephine looked and looked. The man turned the corn with a long stick. He did not touch the fire with his hands.

Then Josephine saw a shiny thing in the grass. It was a broken bottle. She reached out her hand. Grandma caught her fingers right away. "Not that one," grandma said. "Sharp things can hurt you." The man in a green vest came and picked it up with a glove. He put it in a bag.

"Why is the corn so puffy?" Josephine wondered. The man smiled. He gave one warm ear to grandma, and grandma held it with her sleeve. Grandma blew on it, once and twice. Then Josephine took a little bite. It was hot, then just right. "More corn, please!" Josephine begged. Grandma laughed and said, "One more, and then we find the ducks."

activity: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
knowledge_domain: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
story:
Brooklyn went to the bookshop with her dad. She wanted to find a book about cats. "Where do we look?" she asked. Dad said, "Let's look at the letters."

They found a big sign with letters on it. Brooklyn pointed at the first one. "That is B," she said. Dad made the sound. "Buh, buh, B," he said. Brooklyn laughed. "B is for Brooklyn!"

Then something funny happened. Dad said, "Buh, buh." And Brooklyn heard a word. "Book!" she said. "Book starts with B!" Dad clapped. "Yes! The letter B makes the buh sound. So book begins with B."

Brooklyn looked around the shop. What else started with B? She saw a shelf of books. She saw a bear on a cover. "Bear!" she said. "Buh, buh, bear!" A friendly shop lady walked over. "Would you like a cat book?" she asked. Brooklyn thought hard. "Cuh, cuh," she said slowly. "Cat starts with C!"

The lady took Brooklyn to the C shelf. There it was. A little book with a cat on the front. Brooklyn hugged it tight. "Can we spell my name at home?" she asked Dad. Dad smiled. "We can spell it after dinner."

At home, Brooklyn turned to the last page. There was a mirror on it. In the mirror, she saw a girl holding a cat book. Under the mirror were five letters. Brooklyn pointed at each one. "B," she said. "R. O. O. K." She stopped at the last letter. "That one is N!" she shouted. "N is for Nyah!" The cat on the cover seemed to wink at her, and Brooklyn winked right back.

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
knowledge_domain: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
story:
Sara stood by the farm gate with a little bag of seeds. She wanted her own vegetable garden. Grandpa gave her a small patch of dirt near the fence.

Sara dug a little hole. She dropped a seed in. She poured water on top. The water began to sink into the dirt. "Where did it go?" Sara asked. "Down into the ground," said Grandpa. "The seed drinks it."

Sara came back each day. She watered her seeds again and again. The water would sink, sink, sink. Then one morning, Sara saw a green sprout. "Grandpa, look!" she called. "My seed woke up!" Grandpa smiled. "Water it some more," he said. Sara poured the water slowly. A pretty butterfly landed on the fence to watch. "Grow, little plant, grow," said Sara. The sprout stood up tall in the sun.

activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
knowledge_domain: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
story:
Victor wanted to paint a fire truck at school. But the red paint pot was empty. He needed help.

He walked to his teacher. "Can you help me, please?" he asked. Miss Amy smiled. "Yes, I can help you." She opened a big bottle. She began to pour red paint into the pot. Drip, drip, drip. The paint looked like a shiny red river.

Victor sat down to paint. He made a big red fire truck. Then his elbow bumped the water cup. Splash! Water ran across the table and onto Ben's paper. Victor felt his tummy go tight. "I am sorry, Ben," he said. Ben looked at his wet paper. Then he said, "That is okay. Can you help me dry it?" Victor ran to get paper towels. They patted the paper together. Pat, pat, pat. Soon it was dry.

Ben shared his crayons with Victor. "Thank you," said Victor. "Thank you," said Ben. By lunch time Victor was very sleepy. He yawned a big yawn. Miss Amy put his painting on the wall to dry. "Look at your fire truck," she said. Victor looked up and smiled.

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
knowledge_domain: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
story:
Harrison stood on the balcony with Daddy. He held a small pot of dirt. "I want a big garden," he said.

"We can plant three seeds," said Daddy. "One, two, three." Harrison pushed the seeds into the dirt. He patted the soil until it was smooth. Then he watered the pot. Every morning he ran to look. Nothing came up. "Where are my seeds?" he asked.

"Rain makes plants grow," said Daddy. "We can give them rain from the tap." So they watered the pot every day. Soon a tiny green tip peeked out. Harrison pointed at it. "It came up!" he said. More tips came, one, two, three. Daddy helped him write the letter H on the pot. Harrison smiled and gave the little plants one more drink of water.

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
knowledge_domain: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
story:
Joshua's dog Ruff was barking at the door. Ruff's tail wagged and wagged. Joshua felt happy inside. "Grandpa is here!" Dad opened the door. Grandpa held a big red box. Joshua jumped up and down. He felt so excited. "Is that for me?" he asked. "It is," said Grandpa.

Joshua pulled at the ribbon. It would not open. He pulled harder. Then he felt angry. His face got hot. He threw the ribbon on the floor. "It won't open!" he shouted.

Grandpa sat down next to him. "Let's try together," he said. Grandpa held the box. Joshua tugged the ribbon with his teeth. It slipped loose! The box opened. Inside was a cool blue fire truck with a long ladder.

Just then Ruff barked very loud. A clap of thunder boomed outside. Joshua grabbed Grandpa's hand. His tummy felt tight and scared.

The rain came. Joshua could not play outside. A little tear rolled down his cheek. He felt sad.

Grandpa patted the rug. "Trucks can drive in here," he said. Joshua pushed the fire truck across the floor. It went fast. Ruff chased the wheels and barked. Joshua laughed and laughed. The rain tapped on the window, and the ladder clicked up, up, up.

activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
knowledge_domain: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
story: Claire went to Grandma's house. She wanted a house of her own. But Grandma had no little play house. Claire felt sad. Grandma smiled and said, "Look what a blanket can do." Grandma hung a big blanket over two chairs. It made a roof. Claire crawled under it. Now she had a house. Claire put her bear inside too. She wrapped Bear in a small towel. Bear closed his eyes and went to sleep, just like that. Claire patted Bear softly. She sang him a little song. Then she heard a sound outside her blanket house. It went tweet, tweet. Claire peeked out. A bird was on the window. It began to fly in big circles. "Grandma, come see!" said Claire. Grandma came and sat down next to her. They watched the bird together until the last circle, and then the bird flew away.

activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
knowledge_domain: searching for a lost favorite toy
story:
Isaac was in the family car. His toy bunny was gone. "Where did Bunny go?" he asked. He wanted Bunny right now.

Isaac looked under the seat. He looked by his feet. He looked out the window. No Bunny. He turned and turned in his seat. Now his head felt dizzy. "Too much turning," said Dad. Dad pulled the car over. "Let's look together."

The sun was bright. Dad opened the back door. The sun shone inside. And there was a flash of white on the floor. The sunlight had touched something soft. It was Bunny! The sun showed Isaac right where to look.

"Bunny!" Isaac grabbed him fast. He hugged Bunny tight. Dad shut the door and got in. "Home we go," said Dad. "We can have a snack in the kitchen." Isaac held Bunny up to the window. "Look, Bunny, the sun!" he said. The sun made Bunny's ear glow.

activity: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
knowledge_domain: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
story:
Margot sat at the little red table. The tablet lay there, dark and still. She wanted to draw a snowman, but the screen showed nothing. She pressed the edge. Nothing happened. She pressed the back. Still nothing.

"Where is the picture?" Margot asked. Her teacher sat beside her. "Try the round button," she said. Margot found the round button. She pushed it. The screen woke up. It was bright and full of colors. Margot clapped her hands.

She tapped the blue crayon icon. The drawing app opened. She drew a big snowman with a winter hat. Then the teacher said it was time for snack. Margot pressed the button again. The screen went dark. She slid the tablet into its soft gray bag. "I can do it all by myself," she said, and smiled at the bag on the shelf.

activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
knowledge_domain: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
story: Wesley was a small boy in a big forest. He found a soft, round pinecone on the ground. He picked it up. "You are my baby," he said. The pinecone had a scratch on one side. "You need a bandage," Wesley said. He wrapped it in a green leaf. The pinecone looked cozy now. Wesley wanted to make a house for it. He put two sticks in the moss. He laid more sticks across the top. The sticks made a little roof. The pinecone fit under it just right. "Now you have a bed," Wesley said. A chipmunk ran by and stopped. Wesley had an idea. He held the leaf up like a blanket. "Time for night-night," he whispered. He patted the pinecone gently. Then he carried his baby home to show Daddy. "Look, I am the daddy now," Wesley said.

activity: to clap along to the steady beat of a song and sing a nursery rhyme from memory
knowledge_domain: to clap along to the steady beat of a song and sing a nursery rhyme from memory
story:
Gabriella sat on the small red rug. Miss Ada, her music teacher, sat by the piano. "Today we will clap and sing," said Miss Ada. "Watch me first."

Miss Ada played a song. She clapped her hands. Clap, clap, clap. The claps sat right on the beat, like feet walking. Gabriella tried. Her claps went too fast. Then they went too slow. "I can't do it," she said. Her lip wobbled.

"Watch my hands," said Miss Ada. "Clap when my hands come together." Gabriella looked and looked. She clapped when the hands met. Clap, clap, clap. Her claps matched the piano. Then she sang, "Baa, baa, black sheep, have you any wool?" All by herself, with no words on the wall.

At home, Mama let her see a small toy sheep on the shelf. Gabriella clapped and sang the whole rhyme again. "More," she said, and clapped her hands.

activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
knowledge_domain: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
story:
Hazel wants a book about a chicken. She walks to the big shelf. The shelf is too tall. The chicken book sits up high.

Hazel tries to reach it. She stands on her toes. Her fingers touch nothing. A boy is sitting on the floor. She bumps his tower of books. Crash! The books fall down.

"Sorry," Hazel says. The boy nods. He stacks them again. Hazel helps. She hands him each fresh book from the pile.

Then Hazel sees a lady at the desk. She tugs her mom's hand. Mom walks with her. "Please, can you help?" Hazel asks the lady. The lady smiles. She reaches up. She gets the chicken book down.

"Thank you," says Hazel. The book feels smooth. It smells like paper. The boy waves at her from his swing of a chair. Hazel sits by her mom. She opens the book. "Cluck, cluck," says the chicken on page one.

activity: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
knowledge_domain: people's jobs and how a community works
fact: At a library, you can borrow books and take them home, but you must bring them back by a certain day so other people can read them too.
story:
Logan stood at the big library desk. He wanted a book about trucks. But first he needed a card. The librarian typed his name. Then she handed him a small blue card. "Now you can borrow books," she said. Logan held the card with both hands.

He found a truck book on a low shelf. He sat on the floor to look at it. His sock was loose, so he pulled it up over his knee. The pages showed a big red dump truck. Logan wanted to keep it forever.

The librarian stamped a paper inside the book. "Bring it back next week," she said. "Then other kids can read it too." Logan hugged the book tight. "I can bring it back," he said. At home, his mom read it three times. Logan turned the last page himself and said, "Thank you, truck book. See you next week."

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
knowledge_domain: people's jobs and how a community works
fact: At a library, you can borrow books and take them home, but you must bring them back by a certain day so other people can read them too.
story:
Emily was at Grandma's house. On the table was a big red book. "Whose book?" asked Emily. "It is a library book," said Grandma. "We can take it home. But we must bring it back by Saturday. Then other people can read it too."

Emily sat on the soft rug. She held the book. She opened the front cover first. Grandma turned the pages from front to back. On each page were little marks. "Those marks are words," said Grandma. "Words tell the story." Emily touched the marks with one finger. The words said bear, and there was the bear! Emily turned more pages. Front to back, front to back.

Then Emily hugged the book to her neck. "I want to keep it forever," she said. "It is mine." Grandma sat down beside her. "Saturday is coming," she said softly. "The book must go back. Then we can borrow a new one."

Emily felt her eyes go hot. A tear did not fall, but her throat hurt a little. Then Grandma said, "You can pick the next book. Any one you like." Emily looked at the red book. It was slimy where the dog had licked it, so Grandma wiped it clean.

On Saturday, Emily held the book all the way to the library. She gave it to the lady at the desk. Then Emily ran to the shelves. She found a blue book with a duck on it. She opened the front cover first. "Words," said Emily, and turned the pages, front to back. "This one comes home with us. Then it goes back too."

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
knowledge_domain: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Dylan wanted warm milk before bed. He ran to the kitchen. Mama was at the stove. The pot went hiss, hiss, hiss. Steam rose up like a little cloud.

Dylan reached out his hand. "Stop," Mama said. She caught his fingers. "That pot is hot." She turned on the cold tap. Cold water ran over her own hand. Then she touched the pot holder. "See? The cloth keeps my hands safe."

Dylan touched the pot holder too. It was soft and cool. He put a safe step back from the stove. "Can I help?" he asked. "Yes," said Mama. She poured the warm milk into his cup. Dylan held the cup with both hands. It was warm, not hot. He drank it all up.

Then he wanted his crunchy crackers. But the crackers were high up. He looked at the tall shelf. He did not climb. "Mama, please," he said. She smiled and got them down. Dylan stayed close to her feet. He munched his crackers. "Bed soon," said Mama. Dylan gave her a big hug. She held him all the way to his room.

activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
knowledge_domain: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
story:
Stella loved the little play kitchen at school. But today it was empty. No pots. No cups. Where did they go? Ben had taken them to the sand table.

"I need a pot for my soup," Stella said.

Then she saw a big wooden block on the shelf. It was round and fat. "Hello, pot!" she said. She put the block on the toy stove.

Next she needed a baby to feed. She found a sock with a button eye. "Hello, baby!" she said. She wrapped the sock in a small towel.

The baby needed a bed. Stella turned a basket upside down. The basket was soft inside. She laid the sock baby down.

"I am so lucky," said Stella. "This is the best house ever."

Then Stella scratched her chin, like a mama thinking. "Is the soup ready?" she asked. She looked at the block. "Yes it is!" she said. "Time to eat."

Stella picked up the block pot and fed her sock baby first.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
story:
Zoey stood in the garage. Dad had a big drum there. It sat on a box made of wood. "Can I play it?" she asked. "You need soft taps first," said Dad.

Zoey tapped the drum. It went boom. She tapped harder. It went BOOM BOOM. Her dog Max ran under the workbench. "Too loud for Max," said Dad. "He needs quiet ears."

Zoey looked at Max. She tapped very soft. Pum. Pum. Max came out. He sat down near her feet. Zoey tapped soft again. Max wagged his tail. "You like this song," she said. She tapped slow and soft. Pum. Pum. Pum.

Max put his head on her shoe. Dad picked up a little drum too. "May I join?" he asked. Zoey smiled. They played together, soft and slow. Max closed his eyes.

activity: starting the first day of school
knowledge_domain: starting the first day of school
story:
Sienna stood at the school gate. The playground was big and loud. She held her new red cup of bubble soap. "Can I try?" she asked her teacher.

"First dip the wand in," said Miss Ana. "Then blow slow air through the hole." Sienna dipped the wand. It came out wet and shiny. She blew too hard. The soap flew off. No bubble came. She tried again. This time she blew slow, thin air, like a tiny sigh. A round bubble grew. It got bigger and bigger.

"Look! I made it!" said Sienna. The bubble floated up. A boy named Theo ran to see it. It popped on the slide with a little sound. Theo laughed. "Do it again!" he said. Sienna dipped the wand. She blew slow air once more. Two bubbles went up this time, side by side, one small and one big. Theo clapped his hands.

"My turn next," said Theo. Sienna gave him the wand. "Blow slow," she said. "Like this."

activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
knowledge_domain: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story: Adam wants to help at snack time. "Can I put out the cups?" he asks. Ms. Rosa smiles. "Yes. But how many cups do we need?" Adam looks at the rug. He counts his friends. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven." He runs to the shelf. He takes cups, one by one. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven." Seven cups for seven friends. Each friend gets a cup. Nobody is left out. A small green leaf fell off the plant. Adam picks it up. He puts it back in the pot. Then Ms. Rosa brings apple slices. They smell fresh. Adam takes a big bite. Crunch! Then they sing the counting song together, all the way to ten. "Ten!" shouts Adam, clapping his hands.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
story:
Georgia sat with Grandpa in the big chair. The game was on TV. Everyone wore striped shirts, blue and white. Mama wore one too.

Georgia wanted to cheer like the big people. They clapped and yelled when the team ran. But Georgia clapped too early. The room went quiet. Her hands clapped all alone.

"Watch the ball," Grandpa said. So Georgia watched the ball. The ball went this way. Then that way. Then it went through the net. The people on TV jumped up. Then everyone in the room jumped up too.

Georgia waited. She watched the ball again. It ran and ran. Then it went through the net. The people on TV jumped up. Georgia clapped her hands. Everyone clapped too. Mama picked her up. "You cheered at the right time!" said Mama.

Georgia watched some more. The night got dark outside the window. The ball went through the net one more time. Georgia clapped and clapped.

"Again!" said Georgia.

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
knowledge_domain: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Rehmat wanted to find her cat, Milo. He was hiding in the backyard. She called him. "Milo! Milo!" No cat came.

Rehmat looked with her eyes. She saw the big mountain of leaves by the fence. She touched the leaves with her hands. They were soft and a little wet. No Milo there.

Then her ears heard a sound. It was a tiny "meow." It came from the shiny red wagon! Rehmat ran to the wagon. She peeked in with her eyes. There was Milo, curled up and sleeping.

Rehmat smelled something good. Dad was cooking fish on the grill, far away. He waved. "Almost done," he said. Milo woke up. He smelled the fish too. He jumped out of the wagon and ran to Dad.

Milo sat by Dad's feet. He licked his lips with his tongue. Rehmat gave him a tiny taste of fish in his bowl, after Dad said it was cool. Milo ate it all up. Then he rubbed his soft head on Rehmat's hand.

activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
knowledge_domain: searching for a lost favorite toy
story:
Colton went to the grocery store with Mama. He held his soft bunny in his arms. Then Colton saw the big apples. He let go of bunny to touch one apple. Round apples rolled down the pile. When the apples rolled, Colton saw something gray underneath. It was soft. It was bunny!

"Bunny, there you are!" said Colton.

A teacher from Colton's school was there too. She helped pick up the apples. "The apples rolled away when you pulled one," she said with a smile. Colton put the apples back on the pile, one by one.

"Thank you," said the apple man. He gave Colton a thick paper bag. Colton drew on the bag with his crayon while Mama paid. He drew a picture of bunny sitting on the apples.

Mama picked Colton up for a hug. "You found bunny all by yourself," she said.

Colton hugged bunny tight. "No more rolling, apples," he said.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
knowledge_domain: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Leo went to the park with his dad. Leo held his dad's hand. "Stay close," said Dad. Leo wanted to see the ducks.

Leo ran ahead. Dad was far away. Leo looked back. He could not see his dad. He stopped and stood still.

Then he heard his dad call, "Leo!" Dad came close and took his hand. Leo held on tight. Now they could see the ducks together.

Near the ducks was a big grill. A man was cooking corn. Leo saw smoke rise up. The grill looked red and hot. Leo reached out his hand.

Dad caught it right away. "That is hot," said Dad. Dad put his own hand near the air above the grill. Dad pulled it back fast. "Ooh, hot!" said Dad.

Leo put his hand near the air too, far away. He felt warm air on his fingers. Leo pulled his hand back fast, just like Dad. "Hot!" said Leo.

They sat on a rough log. Leo kicked a little stone. It rolled into the grass. Dad gave Leo a cold juice box from the bag. It felt cool in Leo's hands. Leo drank it all up. His tummy felt happy.

"Want more corn?" asked Dad. The man at the grill handed Dad a hot corn stick with a glove. Dad blew on it. Then Leo touched the corn. It was warm, not hot. Leo took a big bite.

"Yum," said Leo. He held his dad's hand all the way home.

activity: to count a group of up to ten objects and say which of two groups has more
knowledge_domain: counting, comparing amounts, and shapes
fact: When you count a group of things, the last number you say tells how many there are. You get the same answer no matter which one you count first.
story:
Peyton sat at the math club table. There were two plates of cookies. She wanted the plate with more cookies. But which one had more?

Miss Joy said, "Count them, Peyton."

Peyton picked a cookie from the red plate. She counted, "One, two, three, four, five." Five cookies!

Her friend Ben said, "Count again, but start from the other end!"

Peyton giggled. She turned the plate around. She counted, "One, two, three, four, five."

"Five again!" she said. "The last number is the same!"

Now she counted the blue plate. "One, two, three, four." Four cookies.

"Five is more than four," said Peyton. She picked up the sweet red plate. "I pick this one!"

Ben laughed. "You counted it two ways, Peyton."

Peyton bit her cookie. "Mmm," she said. "Cookies taste the same from both ends too."

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
story:
Amira stands at the little table. Today she will make bread for her family. The teacher pours flour into the bowl. Amira stirs it with a big spoon. The flour is dry and crumbly. It will not stick. It falls apart in her hands. Amira wants a ball of dough, but she only has a messy pile.

The teacher gives her a cup of milk. Amira pours it in, little by little. She stirs and stirs. Now the flour sticks together. The milk makes the crumbs turn into one soft ball. Amira knows just what to do. She pushes the dough flat with her hands. "Look," she says. "I made it stick!"

She cuts out little sheep shapes with a round cutter. The sheep look so nice with their curly edges. The teacher puts the tray in the hot oven. Amira waits at the safe table. Soon the smell fills the room. Mommy comes in and smiles. "Is one of these sheep for me?" she asks. Amira holds up the biggest one and says, "This sheep is for you, Mommy."

activity: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
knowledge_domain: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
story:
Brielle stood in the nursery room. There was a new little bed. There was a new little blanket. A baby was in the little bed. It was her new baby brother.

Brielle wanted the baby to look at her. She waved her hand. The baby did not look. She made a soft sound. "Ooo," said Brielle. The baby still did not look. She waited. Then she tried again.

Mommy held the baby up. "Say hello," said Mommy. Brielle clapped her hands, very soft. Clap, clap. The baby turned his head. His eyes found Brielle. He made a small smile. "He looked at me!" said Brielle. "He is so cute." The sun came in the window. It made a warm spot on the blanket. The baby blinked at the light. "Hello, baby brother," said Brielle. She clapped again, one more time, very soft. Clap.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
knowledge_domain: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Bennett wanted to help Dad cook outside. Dad had the grill in the backyard. "Can I do a job?" Bennett asked. "Yes," said Dad. "You can carry the cold buns."

Bennett picked up the bun bag. It felt cool and soft in his hands. The grill was hot. Dad said, "Stay back from the grill." Bennett saw the grill puff out smoke. The smoke made the air wiggle. He took one big step away.

Then Bennett saw a tall stick on the ground near the grill. He reached for it. "Stop," said Dad. "Sticks stay out of the fire." Dad picked up the stick himself. He put it in a bucket of water. The water made a hiss. Bennett held his buns tight. "Buns going on now," said Dad. He opened the grill and laid them in. Bennett stayed close and watched the smoke curl up. "Now we wait," said Dad. "I can wait," said Bennett.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
story:
Sebastian went to the library with his mom. Craft day was at the big table. The librarian, Miss Jo, put out paper, glue, and paint.

"One brush, two brushes, three brushes," said Miss Jo. "Pick one to paint with."

Sebastian picked the biggest brush. He wanted to paint a blue dog. He dipped the brush in water. Then he dug the brush into the blue paint. He pulled it across the paper. The line came out thin and pale. The blue was light, like the sky.

He looked at his friend Maya's paper. Her red was dark and bright. Sebastian watched her brush. It was dry. His brush was dripping wet.

So he tried it his way. He dug his brush into the paint with no water at all. The paint was smooth and thick. He pulled it across the paper. Now his blue was dark, like the night sky. The wet brush had made the blue pale. The dry brush made it dark.

Sebastian painted the dog blue, blue, blue. Then he added one ear, two ears, and one waggy tail.

Miss Jo held it up. "A blue dog!" she said.

"He looks like a kitchen mop," said Sebastian.

Everyone laughed softly. Sebastian smiled and painted one more dog, dark blue all over.

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
knowledge_domain: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
story:
Jules sat at the dinner table. His tummy made a hungry sound. "When is the spaghetti coming?" he asked. "Soon," said Dad. Jules was so excited. He kicked his feet under the table.

Then the big pot went clank on the stove. Dad stirred it. Steam went up, up, up. Jules felt happy. But then his tooth hurt a little. He touched it with his tongue. His loose tooth was wiggly. "Ow," he said. His face went sad.

Mom sat near him. "Is your tooth bothering you?" she asked. "A little," said Jules. Then the dog barked loud. Jules jumped. He felt scared for a second. "It is just the doorbell," said Mom. It was Grandma! Jules felt so happy again. But his brother grabbed his cup, and Jules felt angry. He made a big frown.

"Here," said Grandma. She gave him a soft bread roll. The bread was soft, so his tooth did not hurt. Dad set down the spaghetti. It smelled warm and good. Jules took one bite and smiled. "Can we eat like this every night?" he asked. Grandma laughed. "Yes, every night, my love."

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
knowledge_domain: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
story:
Noah waited at the train station. His grandpa was coming to stay for a week. The train was late. Noah held up his sign. It said "Grandpa" in big red letters.

Then the train came in. It made a big wind. The wind blew the sign right out of Noah's hands. "Oh no!" said Noah. The paper flew down the platform. It went too far to reach.

Grandpa stepped off the train. "Where is your sign?" he asked. "The train blew it away," said Noah. He felt sad. Grandpa smiled. "Let's make a new one," he said. "We can make it at home."

At home, Mom helped them paint. Noah painted the word "Grandpa" again. Then he put beans in a bowl. He set the new sign in the bowl. "Now it can't blow away," he said. Grandpa tested it. He blew as hard as he could. The sign wobbled. But it did not fall.

The next week, they went back to the station. Grandpa held the bowl and the sign. "Read it to me," said Grandpa. Noah pointed at each letter. "G-R-A-N-D-P-A!" he said. Grandpa hugged him tight.

activity: starting the first day of school
knowledge_domain: starting the first day of school
story:
Sadie stood in the school hallway. She held her new backpack tight. It had a little red boat on it. Sadie wanted to go in, but the door was shut. It was big and gray and heavy.

Sadie could not reach the handle up high. She looked and looked. Then she saw a round button by the door. It was flat and shiny. She pushed the button with one finger.

The big door swung open all by itself. Sadie walked through. Behind her, a boy saw what she did. He pushed the button too. The door opened for him as well. He smiled at Sadie.

A teacher came to the hallway. "Hello, Sadie," she said. "Come see our room." Sadie hung her new backpack on a little hook. On the table there was a tub of water and some toy boats. Sadie picked up a boat and stirred the water round and round. The little waves went splash, splash.

"My boat can float," said Sadie.

activity: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
knowledge_domain: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
story:
Levi wanted to paint a dragon egg. He looked at the paint pots. "Red, yellow, blue," he said, tapping each one. "Red, yellow, blue." But there was no green pot. His dragon egg needed green, because dragons sleep in green nests.

Miss Ana got him a brush. Levi dipped it in blue. He painted a thin stripe on his egg. Then he dipped the brush in yellow. He swirled it on the blue stripe. The colours squished together. The stripe turned green! Levi blinked. He looked at his brush.

"It made a new colour," he whispered. He mixed red and yellow too. That made orange, like a little sunset. He finished the egg with green and orange stripes.

Miss Ana held it up. "A real dragon egg," she said.

Levi smiled. "Now it will hatch."

activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
knowledge_domain: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
story:
Everett ran to the swing at the playground. The sky was cloudy and soft. But three kids were already in line.

"My turn next," said a girl named Mia. She held the swing rope tight.

Everett wanted to be a dragon. Dragons do not wait in lines. He jumped in front of Mia and grabbed the rope too.

Then Mia let go of the rope. The boy behind her stepped back too. The line went quiet and still. Nobody swung. Everybody just stood.

Everett pulled the swing, but it felt wrong. A dragon swing is only fun if you fly high. He could not fly with everyone standing still and sad.

He let go of the rope. "You can go first," he said.

Mia smiled. She hopped on and pumped her legs. The swing went up, up, up, past the tall tree. "Look at me! I fly!" she called.

When Mia jumped off, she pointed at Everett. "Now it is the dragon's turn."

Everett climbed on. The line behind him clapped and cheered. His swing went up, up, up. He roared a big dragon roar.

"Rawr!" he shouted. "Next friend, come fly!"

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
knowledge_domain: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Wyatt wanted to help Dad cook lunch. But first Dad said, "Stay close to me." Wyatt stayed close to Dad in the backyard.

Dad lit the grill. The grill got hot. Wyatt could feel the heat on his face. He stepped back two big steps. Dad nodded. Wyatt put his milk cup on the table, far from the hot grill. A drop of milk ran down the cup. The table was wet where the milk dripped.

Then Wyatt saw a shiny knife on the grass. He reached for it. Dad said, "Stop. I pick up knives." Dad picked up the knife and put it high on a shelf. Wyatt waved his hand near the grill again. Hot. He waved it near his milk cup. Cold. He touched the wet table. Cool too.

Wyatt stayed close. Dad stayed close. They watched the burgers sizzle together. "Lunch soon," said Dad. Wyatt sat down on his little chair and waited. "I can taste the burgers already," he said. Dad smiled and flipped one over.

activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
knowledge_domain: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Margot sat down at the dinner table. Her plate had ten little meatballs on it. Ten! That was a lot.

"Can I count them?" she asked.

"Of course," said Mama.

Margot touched each one with her fork. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten."

Then she ate one. It was warm and yummy. She counted again. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine."

Only nine now! When she ate one, the number got smaller.

"I pretend I am an owl," said Margot, opening her eyes wide. "Owls count at night. Is the dark scary for owls?"

"Owls love the dark," said Mama. "They watch it all night."

Margot ate another meatball. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight."

Eight. The plate was getting empty. Her tummy was getting full.

She ate and counted all the way down. "One." She popped it in her mouth.

"Zero meatballs left," she said, and held up her empty plate.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
story:
Matthew went to the farmers' market with his dad. They saw red apples and orange carrots. They saw a shiny fish on the ice. "I want to cook dinner," said Matthew. "Okay," said Dad. "Let's pick things."

Matthew picked three big potatoes. He carried them in a little bag. At home, Dad put water in a pot. Dad put the pot on the stove. "You can wash the potatoes," said Dad. Matthew washed them in the sink. The water turned brown. "Look, Dad! The dirt came off!"

Dad peeled the potatoes with a knife. Matthew stood far away and watched. Dad dropped the potatoes into the pot. The pot began to bubble. "The bubbles mean the potatoes are cooking," said Dad. Matthew clapped his hands.

The potatoes got soft. Dad used a fork to mash them. "Now you can add the milk," said Dad. Matthew poured the milk in. The potatoes turned white and fluffy. He mixed and mixed and mixed.

Mom and the baby came to the table. Matthew wore his big apron to serve dinner. Everyone took a big bite. "Mmm," said Mom. "Matthew made this!" Matthew smiled. He passed the shiny spoon to Dad. "More potatoes, please," said Dad. Matthew gave him more.

activity: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
knowledge_domain: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
story:
James was at Grandpa's house. He wanted to play outside in the snow. Grandpa handed him his red coat. "Can you put it on yourself?" Grandpa asked.

James pushed his arms in. But the coat looked wrong. The tag was on his chin. The zipper was on his back. "Hmm," said James. He could not reach it. Grandpa turned him around, so the tag sat at his neck. Now the zipper hung in front, right by his tummy.

James pulled the zipper down. He pushed the little slide into the slot at the bottom. Then he pulled it up, up, up. Zip! The coat closed all the way to his chin. He was warm now, and not thirsty for cold air.

"Grandpa, look! I did it!" said James. "Thank you for waiting," said Grandpa.

Grandpa gave him a sandwich in his pocket. James ran out the door into the snow.

activity: spending a surprise snow day at home
knowledge_domain: spending a surprise snow day at home
story:
Chloe woke up early. She looked out the window. The backyard was all white! "Snow!" she shouted. Mama came to see. "No school today," said Mama. "It is a snow day."

Chloe wanted to play outside fast. She put on her boots. She put on her big red coat. Then she ran out the back door. The snow went crunch, crunch under her boots. It was cold on her nose. She made a snowball with her mittens.

Chloe threw the snowball at the fence. Thump! The snow stuck to the wood. It did not fall down. Chloe laughed. She threw another one. Thump! That one stuck too. The fence was turning white and bumpy.

Mama called, "Come see!" There was a card in the mailbox, a letter from Grandma. Chloe ran inside. Her mittens were wet and snowy. She set them on the warm radiator. Then she watched. Soon the snow on her mittens turned to little wet drops. The mittens got dry and soft. "My mittens are warm," said Chloe. "Can we go back out after snack?"
